definition: A heavier 12 inch LP. Standard weight is about 130-155 grams; 180 gram records use the same stampers and groove depth.
Making metal parts from the lacquer to produce stampers; 3-step adds a metal mother so more stampers can be made for bigger runs.
RCA Victor's 7-inch single at 45 rpm with a large center hole, introduced January 10, 1949.
The Westrex system that cuts left and right channels on the two walls of one groove, each at 45 degrees; the US standard from December 27, 1957.
The stereo groove standard: two channels cut at 45 degrees to the record surface and 90 degrees to each other, so the stylus moves both sideways and up and down.
The shellac-era disc, produced commercially from 1897 to the late 1950s; speeds were not standardized, despite the name.
DVS modes that do (absolute) or do not (relative) track where the needle sits on the record.
An outward bias on the tonearm that cancels skating force; dial numbers do not equal the actual force.
A turntable whose motor turns the platter through a belt.
PVC made with renewable feedstock, such as used cooking oil, in place of petroleum.
A record pressed from a non-PVC plastic, such as Evolution Music's sugar-and-starch recipe.
The lump of PVC placed in the press before it is squeezed into a record.
British Phonographic Industry; publishes official UK sales from Official Charts Company data.
A tiny flat on the cutting stylus that polishes the groove wall; the hot stylus allowed much smaller ones.
The tiny arm that carries the stylus and passes its motion to the cartridge's generator.
The release's number, usually the same on both labels; unlike the matrix number it does not change from side to side.
The wide groove used on most records made before 1948.
A plant's bundled price for a finished record: lacquers, plating, labels, sleeves and a printed jacket.
The PVC mix records are pressed from, sold as pellets. Black comes from carbon black.
The suffix after the dash showing which cut of a side this is, such as -1 or -2.
The transducer that turns the amplified signal into stylus motion, such as the Neumann SX-74.
The small chisel, usually sapphire, in the cutter head that carves the groove.
The first commercial record shape, a tube; Edison conceded to the disc in 1913 and made his last cylinders in 1929.
Taming harsh 's' sounds before cutting, since heavy sibilance can distort the master.
The smooth band between the last groove and the label, also called the runout or matrix area, where codes are stamped or etched.
A triangle plus five digits: a job code used by Monarch and other plants, not proof of one plant.
A turntable whose platter sits on the motor itself, giving high torque and a fast start.
Cutting straight into copper instead of lacquer, which skips the lacquer and its plating.
A user-built music database and marketplace launched in November 2000.
Direct Metal Mastering: cutting straight into a copper-plated master instead of a lacquer.
Software and an audio interface that let a turntable control digital files through timecode vinyl.
Growing nickel onto the silvered lacquer in a chemical bath with electric current to make metal copies of the groove.
A filter that sums low frequencies to mono so the groove avoids large vertical swings.
The deliberate bass cut and treble boost applied when cutting a record, reversed by the phono preamp on playback.
Luminate's measure combining album sales with streams and track downloads.
Hand-scribed into the lacquer vs machine-punched; Discogs asks that the difference go in notes.
The machine that heats compound and pushes it out, like toothpaste, to form the puck.
The first nickel negative pulled off the lacquer, called the master in the UK. Its grooves are ridges. One US plant uses the word for an archive copy instead.
The plating generations off a lacquer: a negative father, a positive mother, then the negative stamper used in the press.
Copies from the first production run; matrix data alone does not prove it.
The excess vinyl squeezed out at the edge during pressing, trimmed off and recycled.
The grading scale used mostly by US sellers and Discogs: M, NM, VG+, VG, G+, G, F, P.
Emile Berliner's flat-disc system, patented November 8, 1887; the ancestor of every record since.
The improved cylinder machine by Bell, Bell and Tainter that replaced tinfoil with wax, patented May 4, 1886.
How closely neighboring grooves are spaced, measured in lines per inch.
How fast the groove passes the stylus: about 21 inches per second at the outer edge of a 12 inch at 33 1/3, about 28.3 at 45.
Running the source and lathe at half speed, an LP at about 16 2/3 rpm, to make high frequencies easier to cut.
A cutting stylus warmed by a wire coil so it softens the lacquer and cuts a quieter, more detailed groove; developed at Columbia in 1948.
A triangle with IAM inside, marking Capitol's Scranton plant about 1963-1973.
Shooting molten plastic into a closed mold, as Sonopress does with PET for its EcoRecord, instead of compressing a PVC puck.
Distortion and loss near the label, where the groove moves slower and wavelengths are shorter.
A certification for sustainable and circular supply chains, used for BioVinyl.
Drying center labels in an oven, often overnight, so moisture does not bubble them in the press.
An aluminum disc coated with nitrocellulose; the master groove is cut into the coating.
Side-to-side and up-and-down motion of the groove; in stereo, music moves the stylus tip in a mix of the two.
A record cut one at a time in real time into a blank of vinyl, polycarbonate or acrylic, with no pressing.
The long-playing 12-inch record at 33 1/3 rpm, unveiled by Columbia in June 1948.
US sales tracker, formerly Nielsen SoundScan; counts consumer purchases rather than RIAA-style shipments.
The machine that turns the blank and moves the cutter head across it.
Source codes on CDs: an L-code added at glass mastering and an IFPI code added at pressing.
The per-side production code in the dead wax that files the stamper and ties it to the right label.
The narrow groove introduced with the 1948 LP; microgroove discs carry nearly twice as many grooves as coarse-groove discs.
Mid (what both channels share) moves the groove side to side; side (their difference) moves it up and down.
A metal positive plated from the father, with grooves like a record, used to grow stampers.
The code showing which mother (the positive metal part) a stamper was made from.
A cartridge with the coils on the cantilever and a fixed magnet; lower output, usually under 2.5 mV, so it needs more gain.
A cartridge with the magnet on the cantilever and fixed coils; typical output about 4-8 mV.
As summarized by Jazz Collector, a nearly perfect record with no obvious wear.
RCA Victor's equalization curve from about 1952, essentially identical to the RIAA curve.
How many generations of metal parts are made between lacquer and press. More steps means more stampers can come from one lacquer.
How many plating generations come before the stamper; more steps give more stampers for bigger runs.
Neighboring grooves running into each other, which can make a record skip.
A device about 20 years older than the phonograph that traced sound waves but could not play them back; Edison reversed its process.
An amplifier that lifts a cartridge's signal to line level and applies the inverse RIAA curve.
Edison's 1877 machine that recorded by pressing a stylus track into tinfoil on a cylinder, later wax; the first device to record and play back sound.
A printed image sealed under a thin clear playing surface on a PVC core.
A fader that changes platter speed to match tempos; plus or minus 8% or 16% on SL-1200 models.
The runout signature of UK cutting engineer George Peckham.
A faint copy of a loud passage heard right before or after it, a risk of tight spacing on lacquer.
The circular indent on the label left by the press; its diameter can point to a plant.
The warm lump of compound placed between the stampers, about three times as thick as the finished record.
Physical and digital album purchases only, without streams.
Polyvinyl chloride, the plastic most records are pressed from.
A repress marker on some matrices.
The UK grading scale, which includes Excellent at roughly Goldmine VG+.
An annual day of shop-only limited releases, first held April 19, 2008.
Recording Industry Association of America; sets US record standards and publishes official US shipment and revenue figures.
The standard disc EQ: bass cut and treble boost when cutting, reversed on playback; time constants 3180, 318 and 75 microseconds.
Low-frequency noise from the turntable's own moving parts that the stylus picks up.
A paid faster turnaround, priced per record.
Moving a record back and forth under the stylus to make rhythmic sounds.
The compound used for 78s: shellac resin with fillers such as clay, slate or limestone, carbon black and cotton fibers. Heavy and brittle.
Spraying a thin conductive silver layer onto the lacquer, the same way a mirror is made, so it can be electroplated.
The inward pull on a pivoted, offset tonearm caused by groove friction.
Holding a record still on a slipmat while the platter spins, then letting go; a workaround on belt-drive decks.
A color effect made by mixing pellets of different colors in one biscuit.
A thin nickel negative, about 145 grams, mounted in the press, one per side. Worn stampers are replaced from the mother.
Letters or numbers showing which stamper pressed the copy, such as EMI's GRAMOPHLTD and Decca's BUCKINGHAM ciphers.
A press whose molds are heated by electrically heated water instead of steam from a gas boiler.
The diamond tip that rides in the groove; its shape (conical, elliptical, Shibata, MicroLine, line contact) sets how much of the groove wall it touches.
The first few records off new stampers, usually four or five, sent to the artist and label for approval before the run.
One of the values (3180, 318 and 75 microseconds) that set the corners of the RIAA curve.
A control record pressed with a tone (1,000 Hz for Serato) that software reads for speed, direction and position.
An older jacket construction with printed paper glued over board.
The downward weight on the stylus in grams, set with the counterweight to the cartridge maker's figure.
The time from an approved order to delivery; one US plant listed 6-8 weeks as standard in 2026.
Using turntables as musical instruments; the term was coined by DJ Babu in 1995.
Automatic widening and tightening of groove spacing to fit the music, driven by a preview signal about a second ahead.
The same album in a different color, cover or retailer-exclusive edition.
As summarized by Jazz Collector, a record showing signs of careful play and slight wear.
The vinyl compound Columbia used for its first LPs, sold as nonbreakable.
The Vinyl Record Manufacturers Association of North America, founded after the 2020 Apollo Masters fire.
The 1949-50 contest between Columbia's 33 1/3 and RCA Victor's 45; it ended with the LP as the album and the 45 as the single.
Slow (wow) and fast (flutter) speed wobble, given as a percentage; lower is better.
